input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-420: Principles of Data Mining. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Real-world datasets are often large and can be stored in either main memory or a database. In this course, students will learn the basic principles and algorithms of data mining. Topics include knowledge discovery process; data exploration and cleaning; and data mining algorithms. The emphasis is on how to use data mining to describe datasets rather than making predictions. Data mining projects and a term paper are required. Prerequisites: CSCI-320 and (STAT-145 or MATH-251 or STAT-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students may not take this course if they have received credit for CSCI-420H or CSCI-620. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[neo4j-graph-data-modeling]
Property graph models represent domain entities as nodes. Relationships connect nodes and have a type and direction. Nodes and relationships can carry properties. Labels group nodes that play a similar domain role. A useful graph model begins from the questions the application must answer. Traversal patterns determine which relationships the application follows. Identity must be explicit when several records may describe the same entity. Constraints and indexes support data integrity and efficient lookup. Direction, cardinality, and update behavior are part of the model.

[postgresql-documentation]
Relational systems organize data with tables, rows, columns, and declared types. Primary keys identify rows, while foreign keys express references between tables. Constraints reject states that violate declared data rules. Queries select, join, aggregate, insert, update, and delete data. Indexes provide additional access paths for selected queries. Transactions group operations into an atomic unit of work. Isolation controls how concurrent transactions observe one another. Schema design separates entities and relationships, while normalization addresses update anomalies. Query planning and physical structures influence performance without changing logical query meaning.

[rit-csci-420]
Real-world datasets are often large and can be stored in either main memory or a database. In this course, students will learn the basic principles and algorithms of data mining. Topics include knowledge discovery process; data exploration and cleaning; and data mining algorithms. The emphasis is on how to use data mining to describe datasets rather than making predictions. Data mining projects and a term paper are required. Prerequisites: CSCI-320 and (STAT-145 or MATH-251 or STAT-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students may not take this course if they have received credit for CSCI-420H or CSCI-620. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: Data mining focuses on extracting meaningful patterns and relationships from large datasets to describe their characteristics rather than forecast future outcomes.
beats.example: A retail company analyzes transaction logs to identify customer purchase frequency and product affinity clusters.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Foundations of Data Mining
beats.visualDirection: Display a split-screen graphic: left side shows a scatter plot of customer purchases over time, right side shows a simple bar chart of top-selling products, with a caption reading 'Descriptive Analysis vs. Predictive Forecasting'.

beats.claim: Real-world datasets are often large and can be stored in either main memory or a database, depending on size, access patterns, and query complexity.
beats.example: A small customer list fits in RAM for rapid iteration, while a national sales database requires a relational system for structured storage and integrity.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Data Storage Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Show a simple diagram comparing a RAM block (labeled 'Main Memory') with a database server (labeled 'Database'), connected by an arrow labeled 'Storage Selection Based on Scale and Access Needs'.

beats.claim: The knowledge discovery process follows a structured sequence of data exploration, cleaning, algorithm application, and result interpretation.
beats.example: Researchers first load a medical dataset, remove duplicate patient records, apply clustering algorithms, and then document disease correlation patterns.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Knowledge Discovery Process
beats.visualDirection: Create a circular flowchart with four labeled stages: 'Data Loading', 'Cleaning', 'Algorithm Application', 'Interpretation', with arrows connecting each stage sequentially.

beats.claim: Data exploration involves examining dataset structure, identifying missing values, and summarizing distributions to prepare for analysis.
beats.example: An analyst uses summary statistics and frequency tables to detect outliers in temperature sensor readings before proceeding to modeling.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Data Exploration Basics
beats.visualDirection: Display a table with columns for 'Metric', 'Value', and 'Status', showing rows for 'Mean', 'Median', 'Missing Count', and 'Outlier Flag' with checkmarks for completed checks.

beats.claim: Data cleaning removes errors, handles missing entries, and standardizes formats to ensure reliable pattern extraction.
beats.example: A dataset with inconsistent date formats is converted to ISO 8601, and null values are imputed using median substitution.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Data Cleaning Techniques
beats.visualDirection: Show a before-and-after data snippet: left side shows messy entries like 'Jan 1, 2023' and 'N/A', right side shows cleaned entries '2023-01-01' and '15.5', with a label 'Cleaning Workflow'.

beats.claim: Property graph models represent domain entities as nodes, with relationships connecting nodes and carrying properties, labels, and direction.
beats.example: A social network graph stores users as nodes, friendships as directed edges, and attributes like 'age' and 'location' as node properties.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Graph Data Modeling
beats.visualDirection: Render a simple graph with three nodes labeled 'User A', 'User B', 'User C', connected by bidirectional edges labeled 'Friend', each node showing a small property box with 'age' and 'role'.

beats.claim: Relational systems organize data with tables, rows, columns, and declared types, using primary keys and foreign keys to maintain structural integrity.
beats.example: A university database stores students in one table and courses in another, linked by a foreign key in an enrollment table.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Relational Data Modeling
beats.visualDirection: Draw two rectangular tables side-by-side: left table 'Students' with columns 'ID', 'Name', 'Major'; right table 'Enrollments' with columns 'StudentID', 'CourseID', 'Credit', with a dashed line connecting them labeled 'Foreign Key Link'.

beats.claim: Data mining algorithms analyze structured data to uncover hidden patterns, groupings, and associations within the dataset.
beats.example: Clustering algorithms segment customers into high-value, medium-value, and low-value groups based on purchase history.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Data Mining Algorithms Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a simple bar chart with three segments labeled 'High Value', 'Medium Value', 'Low Value', and a caption reading 'Algorithm Output: Customer Segmentation'.

beats.claim: Constraints reject states that violate declared data rules, while indexes provide additional access paths for selected queries to improve performance.
beats.example: A 'age' column constraint prevents negative values, and an index on 'email' speeds up user lookup operations.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Constraints and Indexes
beats.visualDirection: Show a database table with a red 'X' over a negative age entry, and a blue arrow pointing to a search bar labeled 'Indexed Column' with a speed icon.

beats.claim: Effective data mining projects require verifying data quality, selecting appropriate models, and documenting findings for reproducibility.
beats.example: A team checks for missing values, validates algorithm output against domain knowledge, and archives the cleaning script for future reference.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List four checklist items with checkboxes: 'Data Quality Verified', 'Model Selected', 'Results Documented', 'Reproducibility Confirmed', with a clean, minimalist design.

learningObjectives: Define the knowledge discovery process and distinguish descriptive data mining from predictive modeling.
Explain core data exploration and cleaning techniques, including handling missing values and normalizing distributions.
Apply graph and relational data modeling principles to structure datasets for efficient analysis and query execution.

input.text: Next, compare the choices involved in Lesson Title: Data Exploration Basics and make the decision criteria explicit. Data mining projects and a term paper are required. Consider this worked case: An analyst uses summary statistics and frequency tables to detect outliers in temperature sensor readings before proceeding to modeling. On screen, display a table with columns for 'Metric', 'Value', and 'Status', showing rows for 'Mean', 'Median', 'Missing Count', and 'Outlier Flag' with checkmarks for completed checks. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

Use Lesson Title: Data Mining Algorithms Overview to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. In this course, students will learn the basic principles and algorithms of data mining. Consider this worked case: Clustering algorithms segment customers into high-value, medium-value, and low-value groups based on purchase history. On screen, display a simple bar chart with three segments labeled 'High Value', 'Medium Value', 'Low Value', and a caption reading 'Algorithm Output: Customer Segmentation'. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

Stress-test the reasoning around Lesson Title: Relational Data Modeling with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Relational systems organize data with tables, rows, columns, and declared types. Consider this worked case: A university database stores students in one table and courses in another, linked by a foreign key in an enrollment table. On screen, draw two rectangular tables side-by-side: left table 'Students' with columns 'ID', 'Name', 'Major'; right table 'Enrollments' with columns 'StudentID', 'CourseID', 'Credit', with a dashed line connecting them labeled 'Foreign Key Link'. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

Apply Lesson Title: Data Cleaning Techniques to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Constraints reject states that violate declared data rules. Consider this worked case: A dataset with inconsistent date formats is converted to ISO 8601, and null values are imputed using median substitution. On screen, show a before-and-after data snippet: left side shows messy entries like 'Jan 1, 2023' and 'N/A', right side shows cleaned entries '2023-01-01' and '15.5', with a label 'Cleaning Workflow'. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

Begin by framing Lesson Title: Foundations of Data Mining as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. The emphasis is on how to use data mining to describe datasets rather than making predictions. Consider this worked case: A retail company analyzes transaction logs to identify customer purchase frequency and product affinity clusters. On screen, display a split-screen graphic: left side shows a scatter plot of customer purchases over time, right side shows a simple bar chart of top-selling products, with a caption reading 'Descriptive Analysis vs. Predictive Forecasting'. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

With the foundation in place, examine how Lesson Title: Knowledge Discovery Process operates in a concrete sequence. Topics include knowledge discovery process; data exploration and cleaning; and data mining algorithms. Consider this worked case: Researchers first load a medical dataset, remove duplicate patient records, apply clustering algorithms, and then document disease correlation patterns. On screen, create a circular flowchart with four labeled stages: 'Data Loading', 'Cleaning', 'Algorithm Application', 'Interpretation', with arrows connecting each stage sequentially. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

Examine the tradeoffs in Lesson Title: Graph Data Modeling, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Property graph models represent domain entities as nodes. Consider this worked case: A social network graph stores users as nodes, friendships as directed edges, and attributes like 'age' and 'location' as node properties. On screen, render a simple graph with three nodes labeled 'User A', 'User B', 'User C', connected by bidirectional edges labeled 'Friend', each node showing a small property box with 'age' and 'role'. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Now define Lesson Title: Data Storage Foundations precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Real-world datasets are often large and can be stored in either main memory or a database. Consider this worked case: A small customer list fits in RAM for rapid iteration, while a national sales database requires a relational system for structured storage and integrity. On screen, show a simple diagram comparing a RAM block (labeled 'Main Memory') with a database server (labeled 'Database'), connected by an arrow labeled 'Storage Selection Based on Scale and Access Needs'. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.

Connect Lesson Title: Constraints and Indexes to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Indexes provide additional access paths for selected queries. Consider this worked case: A 'age' column constraint prevents negative values, and an index on 'email' speeds up user lookup operations. On screen, show a database table with a red 'X' over a negative age entry, and a blue arrow pointing to a search bar labeled 'Indexed Column' with a speed icon. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.

Finish with Lesson Title: Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Queries select, join, aggregate, insert, update, and delete data. Consider this worked case: A team checks for missing values, validates algorithm output against domain knowledge, and archives the cleaning script for future reference. On screen, list four checklist items with checkboxes: 'Data Quality Verified', 'Model Selected', 'Results Documented', 'Reproducibility Confirmed', with a clean, minimalist design. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
